narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 53.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the fourth decile instead of the average fifth-to-sixth decile among accepted students signaled weaker academic performance in the later stages of your studies. Family income was the second most important factor and also nudged the outcome toward rejection. Although upper-middle income is common among accepted applicants, in your specific profile it contributed negatively. Your LSAT score was the third strongest driver, but this time it worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. Still, at 30 compared to an average of 37 among accepted students, it was not strong enough to overcome the other signals.

Taken together, these pieces of information led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your academic performance in later years and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Strengthening those two areas should meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
